items.followUp: Sketch the speed-time graph of a body moving at constant speed.

rubric.why: Identifies that speed changes with time.
rubric.description: Recognises variable speed on the graph.
rubric.how: State that the graph is not a horizontal line because the speed changes with time; it may be inclined or curved, depending on the motion's pattern of change. A horizontal line represents constant speed.

rubric.why: Describes the graph's shape rather than confusing it with a constant-speed graph.
rubric.how: Describe the graph as a non-horizontal line or curve; a straight inclined line applies when speed changes uniformly.

modelAnswer: The speed-time graph is non-horizontal because the speed changes with time.
It may be an inclined straight line if the speed changes uniformly, or a curve if the change is non-uniform.

items.followUp: Give two examples in which friction is useful in everyday life.

rubric.why: Provides one valid situation in which friction is useful.
rubric.how: Name a suitable example, such as walking, writing, applying brakes, or gripping an object.

rubric.why: Provides a second valid situation in which friction is useful.
rubric.how: Name a different suitable example, such as walking, writing, applying brakes, or gripping an object.

modelAnswer: Friction between our feet and the ground enables us to walk without slipping.
Friction between the brake pads and a wheel helps to stop a vehicle.

items.followUp: Which is greater: sliding friction or rolling friction? Give one reason.

rubric.why: Distinguishes sliding friction by the type of motion involved.
rubric.how: State that sliding friction acts when one surface slides over another.

rubric.why: States the key comparison between the two types of friction.
rubric.how: State that rolling friction is less than sliding friction.

modelAnswer: Sliding friction acts when one surface slides over another.
Rolling friction acts when an object rolls over a surface and is less than sliding friction.

items.followUp: Why can a passenger fall forward when a moving bus stops suddenly?

rubric.why: Identifies inertia as the cause of the passenger's continued motion.
rubric.how: State that due to inertia, the body tends to continue in its state of motion when the bus suddenly stops.

rubric.why: Connects the sudden change in bus motion to the danger of falling from the roof.
rubric.how: Explain that the passenger may be thrown or fall off the roof, especially when the bus stops, starts, or turns suddenly.

modelAnswer: Due to inertia, a passenger's body tends to continue in its state of motion when the bus stops, starts, or turns suddenly.
The passenger may therefore be thrown off the roof, making roof travel dangerous.

items.followUp: State the second condition of equilibrium and write its mathematical formula.

rubric.why: States that the resultant force must vanish for translational equilibrium.
rubric.description: States the first condition of equilibrium.
rubric.how: State that the vector sum of all forces acting on a body is zero.

rubric.why: Provides the mathematical expression of the first condition.
rubric.how: Write ΣF = 0 or an equivalent formula for zero resultant force.

modelAnswer: The first condition of equilibrium is that the resultant force acting on a body is zero.

items.followUp: How does lowering a vehicle's centre of gravity improve its stability?

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of vehicle height on the centre of gravity.
rubric.description: Relates low vehicle height to a low centre of gravity.
rubric.how: State that keeping the vehicle low lowers its centre of gravity.

rubric.why: Explains the resulting improvement in stability.
rubric.how: Explain that a lower centre of gravity makes the vehicle more stable and less likely to topple, especially when turning.

modelAnswer: The height of a vehicle is kept as low as possible to keep its centre of gravity low.
A low centre of gravity makes the vehicle more stable and less likely to topple when turning.

items.followUp: Why is solar energy considered a renewable source of energy?

rubric.why: Explains that fossil fuels take a very long time to form.
rubric.description: States the formation timescale of fossil fuels.
rubric.how: State that fossil fuels form over millions of years, or extremely slowly.

rubric.why: Explains why their supply cannot be replenished on a human timescale.
rubric.description: Explains why fossil fuels are non-renewable.
rubric.how: State that their reserves are limited and are used much faster than they can form.

modelAnswer: Fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
They are used much faster than they can be formed, so their supply is limited and cannot be renewed on a human timescale.

items.followUp: Define tensile stress and tensile strain, then write the expression for Young's modulus.

rubric.why: Identifies Young's modulus as the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain.
rubric.description: States the definition of Young's modulus.
rubric.how: State that Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, within the elastic limit.

rubric.why: Gives the formula relating Young's modulus to stress and strain.
rubric.how: Write Y = tensile stress / tensile strain; equivalently, Y = FL/(AΔL).

modelAnswer: Young's modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit.
